hints.text: Fast running, vaulting, and dodging use separate keys. The Movement lesson lists your bindings. Practice each one on safe ground before a fight needs it.
Advanced movement drains stamina fast. Running in with an empty bar means standing still when it counts. Leave enough for the escape, not just the approach.
Close on a ranged attacker from behind solid cover. The open ground leaves you a target with nowhere to step back to. Cover first, then the approach.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Pick your exit before the fight starts. Retreat is where fights go wrong. Backing into another room or another group turns it into a trap.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Check around a corner before you chase anyone through it - the next room has its own problems.
When enemies arrive together, don't commit immediately. Pull back until you can see all of them. Crowded ground works against you as much as against them.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Fight where you have room to move, because a narrow doorway becomes a trap the moment they reach you from both sides.
Keep food and escape supplies within reach. A full inventory takes time to search. That is time you don't get back mid-fight.
Find the shooter before you charge; the nearest enemy isn't always the one firing at you.
Eat and sort your bags behind cover. Standing still in a ranged enemy's sight is a free shot. Keep the line broken.
Get distance and solid blocks between yourself and anything about to go off.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Keep explosive work away from supplies you can't replace, and leave yourself a clear way out before you light it.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Look at the descent before you step off, and leave a way back up. A staircase down is a staircase home.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Look at where you'll land before you jump, and work back from edges when you're sorting bags. The drop is unforgiving either way.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Feather Falling and similar protection soften a bad landing, not a bad decision. Check the boots before you rely on them.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Water Breathing runs on a timer and the swim back counts against it. Night Vision won't keep you breathing. Turn around early.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Plan your route back to air before you dive - the return trip is the one that drowns people.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Underwater mining and building is a long job, not a swim. Bring real breathing protection before you settle in.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Fire Resistance helps against fire and lava. Only while it's running, though. Check the effect is active before a hot crossing.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Build the crossing before you carry anything across it, and keep the return path in sight the whole way.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Get clear of the fire before you fight or loot - walking back into the flames undoes the health you just bought.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Leave room to move under sand and gravel; overhead material comes down faster than you can step back.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Damage that keeps arriving after the fight is an effect, not a bug. Check what's on you. The attacker can be long gone while the effect works.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Wither keeps working whether you fight or not, so reach a safe place first.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Milk clears every effect you have. That includes the ones keeping you alive. Check your timers before you drink.
Pack food before a long trip and hold a reserve for the walk home.
sources: minecraft@1.20.1: LivingEntity, Player, FoodData, DamageSources, MobEffects, EnchantmentHelper

hints.text: Food builds nutrition groups, not just a full hunger bar. Tooltips say what each food adds, so eat different things as you find them and pack a mix.
Food groups run down slowly over a long trip. Open the nutrition screen to see which is low. Then eat something that adds to it.
Sugar borrows from your other food groups. When the boost fades, eat real food instead of more sugar, or the crash just cycles.
Frozen food won't feed you until it thaws. A frozen main supply is no supply at all. Keep an edible backup for cold trips.
Merging stacks can change a food's temperature, and warming isn't thawing. Check the tooltip before the first bite.
Tooltips show spoilage and temperature as well as nutrition. Check stored provisions before you pack for a trip.
Purity 3 is safe to drink. Lower needs more cleaning. Check before you trust a bottle, including the one in your auto-drink slot.
The extra water slot drinks for you, but only from what you load into it. Keep it filled with safe water. Watch it run out.
A Rain Collector needs open sky above it. A roof stops collection, even when the rest of your water station is sheltered.
Rain comes and goes, and the collector fills up. Bottle the surplus and keep empty bottles. You'll have a reserve between showers.
A filled collector is a drink in your hand or a bottle in your pack. Either way, check purity first.
Armor stops blows. Cold insulation stops the cold. Check a garment's temperature protection before you head into freezing ground.
Heat works the same way. Check what your clothing actually protects against before you cross hot country.
Your body temperature and the air's are different readings. Recovery happens at one of them. Check both when you're choosing where to stop.
A prepared waterskin pushes your body temperature the other way. Check its temperature before you rely on it.
Long routes cross weather. Plan stops in milder ground, and pack for where you're going rather than where you started.
Set your shelter while the weather is still mild. A clear walk out doesn't promise a clear walk back. Plan the return while you can.
Don't let an exposed worksite be your only shelter. Wait the storm out somewhere safer, then check conditions before crossing open ground.
An assault warning is your preparation time. Repair equipment and top up food. Finish those jobs before the attackers arrive.
When the warning sounds, walk your base's approaches. Decide where defenders stand and where they can fall back.
Agree on the plan while there's time: where to defend, when to leave. A fortified entrance still needs an exit behind it.
ChemLib gases escape from stored items into the air. Released gas joins the pollution system. Contain stockpiles before they're a problem.
A carried gas supply is inventory with consequences. Inspect the material before you treat it like ordinary cargo.
Hosted radioactive ore can sit inert until you mine it. Ore, concentrate, and finished forms don't behave alike. Check what you're holding.
Putting mined radioactive material back down doesn't make it inert again. Handling requirements follow the material, not the block.
Lessons are there from the start. A fast join doesn't cost you them. Everything on the loading screens stays in Threads.
Press {threads} to open Threads during play. Lessons live there too, so an instruction is never more than a keypress away.
Better Content changes a lot of recipes. Open EMI before you gather. Carrying the wrong materials home is the expensive way to learn that.
Check an item's uses as well as its recipe - one material often feeds several processes.
Multi-step recipes run ordered passes over a partly finished item. Follow it in EMI to see the sequence and repeat count. Build the line after that.
Check output counts and process type before you commit. A recipe's machine isn't interchangeable with a similar-looking one.
Before a big build, compare the routes. A recipe using materials you already have may suit the job better.
Life points last until you die. The Life screen shows exactly what each point changes. Read it before you spend one.
Death hands your Life points back. Take a moment to plan the next build instead of repeating the last one.
Choose Life improvements for what you actually plan to do, and check the resulting properties rather than trusting the aspect name.
A Hand Crank runs a small Create setup by hand. Start with the one machine you need, then connect its rotation.
Andesite Alloy has more than one recipe. Compare them in EMI before you build a machine for one of them.
Some worlds past a Dimensional Font hold what a Tinkers' smeltery needs. Look up grout in EMI before you choose a destination.
Repair before you replace, and before a long trip. Check the station's result before you take the tool back.
Ore signs on the surface point at what's below. One deposit can sit in several kinds of stone. Follow the signs, not a single rock color.
Keep the small chunks you dig up. Ones from the same deposit family combine into a full chunk. Unrelated samples never will.
Every ore needs its own separation steps. Most yield more than one material. Check the outputs in EMI before you build the machines.
Processing gives you side materials as well as metal, so leave storage room for everything the recipe makes.
Compare processing routes for the material you actually need. The highest primary yield isn't always the best deal.
Chunk, crushed, concentrate - different stages, different machines. Keep them distinguishable in storage or you'll reprocess something by mistake.
A Dimensional Font drops you in another world. Work out how you'll get home. Pack for the trip before you step through.
The vanilla End route is gone in Better Content. Dimensional Fonts are how you reach the other realms.
Heat pipes share heat with their neighbours, and a hot run needs somewhere to shed it. Trace the line when a section won't cool.
Pressure Chamber recipes need enough pressure and sometimes several items at once. Check both in EMI before you start the process.
Ars Nouveau applies glyphs in the order you write them. When a spell misbehaves, check the sequence - and test changes on something safe.
Relics grow through their own abilities. Read what yours does, then use it where that ability applies.
Carrying a relic may not be enough to trigger it. Check the activation conditions before you count on it.
Check which season a crop is fertile in before you commit a field to it.
Store the surplus while your crops are productive, because a change of season changes what grows well.
A chunk anchor keeps its area running while you're away, as long as it's supplied. Check its fuel before you leave. It gives no warning when the supply runs out.
A working anchor holds a three-by-three chunk area. Build what you want running inside that area, not next to it.
Redstone switches an anchor off, and each variant takes a different resource. Match the supply to what you built before you blame the anchor.
An unattended workshop needs more than one fuel run. An anchor that runs dry stops everything it was holding up. Design the replenishment in.
A published schematic keeps a build's design, not its blocks. Plan to gather materials again when you rebuild it.
Save a design to the schematic library if you want it to outlast the world - including a successor world.
Give an AE2 network a pattern and it learns the recipe. From there a future workshop can make familiar supplies on request. Teach it once.
A pattern teaches the recipe, not the ingredients. Check what the network is missing before you confirm a request.
Roads link settlements through the wilderness, and following one is a good way to find somewhere new.
Village markets want the right trading-spirit colors, so check a merchant's trade before you go collecting.
Creating Space can take you past the sky to Earth orbit. Before a launch, know your destination, your engine's power, and your fuel range.
A World Condenser can start a successor world. Its interface spells out what the reset costs before you commit.
Dimensional Fonts reach more than the Overworld - Ratlantis ruins and Bumblezone hives are out there, each worth a prepared expedition.
One ore family can open several routes. Better processing gives you reasons to revisit deposits you've already found.
A relic's first ability is rarely its last. Using one is how its next development arrives.
A spell is something you write. Glyphs combine a way of casting with a sequence of effects - and there's room to invent.
Rail Beetles survey new routes at a railway's end. One parked mid-line is still in driving mode.
Load rails, supports, and fuel before you ask a Beetle to build. The prompt names what's missing. Stone supports also keep burnable material out of the track.
A Beetle plans only through ground the game has loaded. It won't tunnel rock or route underwater. Explore and clear the way first.
Stop the Beetle and set its brakes before servicing engines or modules. With an empty engine it burns cargo fuel instead.
A Beetle can't take two upgrades of the same kind, so fill each slot with something different.
Long-range dispatch only reaches machines that are already loaded - it won't keep distant chunks running by itself.
Fuel use climbs with speed. A train pushed to its limit burns far more than one running near normal. Choose your speed on purpose.
Budget fuel for the whole round trip - faster is shorter, and sometimes much more expensive.
Shafts, cogs, gearboxes, and belts all spend your stress. Transmission is part of the cost. Count them before you blame the power source.
Long belt runs spend more stress than short ones, so check the span between pulleys when a network overloads.
Rotation carried a long way costs you; a power source close to its machines runs more.
Player Traces carry notes and gestures left by earlier visitors. Open Trace Sight to read them. The marker is worth as much as the text.
Traces hang on their supporting block - change the ground and they're gone.
Trace notes are player writing. Treat their advice as someone's observation, not a pack guarantee.
Bumblezone plants are worth more than one meal. Bring propagation materials home. That's how a farm starts.
Collect several cultivars while you're there, so future meals have options.
Living Pollen Nurseries drop seeds when you break them. Take some home for the garden.
Ratlantis carries the parts for scalable logistics. Check which component your next setup needs. Plan the trip around that, not around the loot.
An automated replanting rat needs the right planting input. An edible harvest isn't always it. Check what the crop or tree actually replants from.
Ratlantis can supply a transport network you haven't built yet, and its rats can replant what they harvest. Hand-carrying everything has an end date.
Route Beacons can point a Rail Beetle where you want to go. A railway doesn't have to follow its first suggestions.
Rail Beetles accept drives for several power systems. A future railway can run on more than furnace fuel.
Gases and radioactive forms give advanced storage its own engineering problems - some of them thermal as well as hazardous.
A faster railway needs a bigger fuel budget. Trading travel time for fuel is a choice, not a failure.
The road to space runs through an engineering table, an electrolyzer, and an air liquefier. The alloys that follow are worth planning for.
You're at Death's Door and can't heal yet. Another hit can kill you. Get to safety - Body shows when healing returns and what you're carrying.
You can heal now. Restore health before the next hit - healing won't clear injuries. Body shows how to treat them.
Empty health puts you at Death's Door instead of killing you outright. The next hit can. Heal for health, treat injuries in Body.
You have medicine for one of your injuries. Reach safety, open Body, pick the injury, and finish the treatment.
Every hit on an existing injury makes it worse while the trauma lasts. Break contact and treat it in Body.
Body lists your injuries and the medicine each needs. One medicine per injury. Totems won't save you from any of it.
Your sugar boost has turned into a crash. Recover somewhere safe and eat real food - more sugar just extends the cycle.
Alcohol is dulling your control right now, so let it clear before you climb, swim, or fight.
One of your food groups is running low. Open the nutrition screen to see which, then eat something that adds to it.
The food in your hand is frozen - thaw it first, because its temperature travels with it.
A campaign is on its way. Cover, supplies, and an exit - set them up before the attackers arrive.
The attackers are here. Work cover and an exit route, and keep your supplies managed through the fight.
You made it through. Check for injuries, replace what you spent, and repair the defenses before you leave again.
Your health is low. Find cover and heal before the next hit, and check Body for injuries healing won't remove.
